This article summarizes a local benchmark run for `ahocorasick`. The benchmark
uses long English and Chinese novels as input, then compares three tasks:

- `detect`: return whether each document contains at least one pattern.
- `count`: return the total number of pattern matches per document.
- `extract`: materialize the extracted matches.

The benchmark compares `ahocorasick` with `polars`, `AhoCorasickTrie`, a basic
base R `for` loop, `tidyverse` + `stringr`, and `data.table`.

## Reproducing

The benchmark data and runners live under `bench/`. Generated output is written
to `bench/output/`, which is ignored by git.

```{bash}
#| label: run-benchmarks
#| eval: false

Rscript bench/01-generate-benchmark-data.R
Rscript bench/02-run-benchmarks.R
```

The results below come from a run with 5 iterations per expression, 200
documents per corpus, and 5000 characters per document chunk.

  | Case              | Corpus     | Patterns | Documents | Input MiB |
  | ----------------- | ---------- | -------- | --------- | --------- |
  | `en_small_common` | `en_docs`  | 32       | 200       | 0.95      |
  | `en_large_rare`   | `en_docs`  | 256      | 200       | 0.95      |
  | `zh_small_common` | `zh_docs`  | 32       | 200       | 2.82      |
  | `mix_medium`      | `mix_docs` | 64       | 200       | 1.89      |

The English corpus is built from *Crime and Punishment*, *Pride and Prejudice*,
and *The Count of Monte Cristo*. The Chinese corpus is built from `红楼梦`,
`鲁迅全集`, `三体1-3`, and `射雕英雄传`.

## Semantics

The benchmark uses fixed-string matching semantics. `ahocorasick` uses a
prebuilt automaton in every timed query. `count` and `extract` use overlapping
matches.

`AhoCorasickTrie` is ASCII-only, so it is skipped for Chinese and mixed UTF-8
cases. `polars` participates in all three tasks. For `extract`, it uses
`extract_many(..., overlapping = TRUE)` and returns a list-column of matches.
`ahocorasick` returns a long data frame through `ac_extract_df()`, so the
`extract` timings include different result materialization costs.

The correctness gate checks all supported `detect` and `count` results against
`ahocorasick`. For `extract`, it checks extracted-match counts per document. All
supported methods agreed in this run.

## Build Cost

`ahocorasick` builds a reusable automaton before querying. Build time was small
for all tested pattern sets.

  | Case              | Build median ms |
  | ----------------- | --------------- |
  | `en_small_common` | 0.24            |
  | `en_large_rare`   | 0.32            |
  | `zh_small_common` | 0.27            |
  | `mix_medium`      | 0.39            |

## Detect

`ahocorasick` was the fastest method for `detect` in all four cases. The base R
loop was close for `en_small_common` because it can stop at the first common
pattern in each document. That shortcut does not hold for larger or rarer
pattern sets.

Median time in milliseconds:

  | Case              | `ahocorasick` | `polars` | `AhoCorasickTrie` | base `for` | `tidyverse` | `data.table` |
  | ----------------- | ------------- | -------- | ----------------- | ---------- | ----------- | ------------ |
  | `en_small_common` | 0.17          | 2.21     | 20.04             | 0.21       | 2.30        | 1.05         |
  | `en_large_rare`   | 0.71          | 2.76     | 5.34              | 21.34      | 25.88       | 18.58        |
  | `zh_small_common` | 0.29          | 2.02     | skipped           | 1.85       | 4.84        | 3.40         |
  | `mix_medium`      | 0.21          | 1.95     | skipped           | 1.27       | 6.10        | 4.21         |

## Count

`ahocorasick` was also the fastest method for `count` in all four cases. This is
where a reusable automaton matters most: repeated fixed-string scans have to
scan the documents once per pattern, while Aho-Corasick can scan once for the
whole pattern set.

Median time in milliseconds:

  | Case              | `ahocorasick` | `polars` | `AhoCorasickTrie` | base `for` | `tidyverse` | `data.table` |
  | ----------------- | ------------- | -------- | ----------------- | ---------- | ----------- | ------------ |
  | `en_small_common` | 2.30          | 27.79    | 21.20             | 20.97      | 6.07        | 4.44         |
  | `en_large_rare`   | 1.96          | 222.25   | 5.64              | 156.14     | 24.54       | 18.96        |
  | `zh_small_common` | 4.74          | 36.33    | skipped           | 81.88      | 12.87       | 9.99         |
  | `mix_medium`      | 3.63          | 57.07    | skipped           | 107.27     | 11.72       | 10.15        |

## Extract

`extract` measures the cost of materializing match results, not just searching.
Here `polars` is the fastest method in all four cases. It returns a list-column
of extracted matches directly from its Aho-Corasick path. `ahocorasick` remains
much faster than the R-level fixed-string baselines, but its current public
`ac_extract_df()` path pays a noticeable R-side reshaping cost.

Median time in milliseconds:

  | Case              | `ahocorasick` | `polars` | `AhoCorasickTrie` | base `for` | `tidyverse` | `data.table` |
  | ----------------- | ------------- | -------- | ----------------- | ---------- | ----------- | ------------ |
  | `en_small_common` | 58.68         | 9.11     | 26.14             | 840.24     | 731.86      | 733.70       |
  | `en_large_rare`   | 40.46         | 3.89     | 5.47              | 274.58     | 146.85      | 149.62       |
  | `zh_small_common` | 51.10         | 8.60     | skipped           | 989.10     | 550.37      | 545.13       |
  | `mix_medium`      | 53.48         | 8.94     | skipped           | 1586.91    | 1106.22     | 1062.91      |

## Why `polars` Can Win On Extract

The `extract` result does not mean that `ahocorasick` is generally slower at
searching. The main difference is in the public result shape and how much work
happens on the R side after the underlying matcher finishes.

There are several important differences:

- `polars` and `ahocorasick` both sit on top of Rust implementations, but
  `polars` returns a native list-column of matches while `ahocorasick` returns a
  long data frame through `ac_extract_df()`.
- `AhoCorasickTrie` is specialized for ASCII input. It does not support UTF-8
  matching, so it cannot cover the Chinese and mixed workloads.
- It builds and searches inside one C++ call. The benchmark cannot separate its
  build cost from query cost, but it also avoids a reusable R-side automaton
  object.
- Its extract result is a nested list of keywords and offsets. `ac_extract_df()`
  returns a long data frame with `doc_id`, matched text, and pattern values.
- The current `ac_extract_df()` implementation calls `ac_extract()` first,
  creates per-document data frames, and then flattens them. That R-side
  reshaping is expensive when many matches are returned.

A diagnostic local check supports this interpretation. On `en_large_rare`, the
internal Rust extraction call took about 2 ms, while public `ac_extract_df()`
took about 42 ms. On `en_small_common`, the internal call took about 6 ms,
while `ac_extract_df()` took about 67 ms. In the full benchmark, `polars`
extract landed at about 4 ms on `en_large_rare` and about 9 ms on
`en_small_common`, which is much closer to the raw matcher cost. The search
itself is fast; the public result construction is the current bottleneck.

This points to a clear optimization target: implement a direct data-frame path
for `ac_extract_df()` that avoids constructing the intermediate list of
per-document data frames.

## Takeaways

Use `ahocorasick` when you need fast reusable multi-pattern matching over R
character vectors, especially with UTF-8 text. In this run it is consistently
fastest for `detect` and `count`.

For `extract`, `polars` is currently the fastest option in this benchmark if a
list-column result fits your workflow. `ahocorasick` is still much faster than
the R-level fixed-string baselines, but `ac_extract_df()` has avoidable R-side
materialization overhead.
